meta.subtitle: Deposition, etch and clean equipment maker; FY26 revenue $23.2B (+26%), gross margin 50.5%, but a 52x trailing P/E prices in much of the AI upcycle.

analystCommentary: The sell-side consensus is Strong Buy: of 35 analysts, 29 rate the shares Buy, 6 Hold and none Sell, with a consensus target of $373.13 — {+ +23.6% +} above the $301.83 close — a median of $380.00 and a range of $290.00 to $500.00. Our BUY sits a notch below that enthusiasm. FY26 delivered {+ +26.0% +} revenue growth, gross margin of 50.5% and diluted EPS of $5.76, and the balance sheet carries net cash; those support a constructive call. But the shares trade at 52.4x trailing earnings, the forward estimates embed a steep ramp — consensus FY27 revenue of $34.9B implies roughly a 50% jump — and 34% of FY26 revenue shipped to China, where trade restrictions are a live risk. We therefore weight a probability-weighted fair value modestly above the current price rather than up at the Street's target, and reserve the upper half of our range for the case where the AI-driven equipment cycle runs longer than a normal upcycle.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Lam Research Corporation designs, manufactures and services wafer fabrication equipment used to build integrated circuits, and describes itself as a global supplier of that equipment to the semiconductor industry. Its core competency is in deposition, etch and clean process technologies, spanning product families the 10-K names such as the ALTUS, SABRE and VECTOR deposition systems and the Akara, Kiyo and Vantex etch systems. The company was incorporated in 1980 and is headquartered in Fremont, California, and sells to memory, foundry and integrated-device manufacturers. It reports as a single business. In FY26 (the year ended June 28, 2026) revenue reached $23.2B, split between systems revenue of $14,885,488 thousand — new leading-edge equipment — and customer support-related revenue and other of $8,347,202 thousand, a stream of services, spares and upgrades tied to the installed base.

thesis.body: Lam sits in the deposition, etch and clean part of wafer fabrication equipment, and FY26 shows an operator gaining scale and margin at once: revenue grew {+ +26.0% +} to $23.2B, gross margin expanded {+ +180 bps +} to 50.5%, and diluted EPS rose {+ +38.8% +} to $5.76. The customer mix tilted toward foundry, which reached 54% of revenue, up 900 basis points. The balance sheet is net cash, and the company returned $3.85 billion through buybacks and $1.27 billion in dividends during the year. The case for owning the shares is that the AI-driven build-out of semiconductor capacity keeps equipment spending elevated, and that Lam's installed base and support revenue smooth the cycle. The case against paying up is that the shares already trade at 52.4x trailing earnings, the consensus forward estimates embed a steep ramp, and the industry is cyclical — revenue fell {- -14.5% -} as recently as FY24. Our BUY backs the constructive case while sizing the bear on cyclicality.

catalysts: Consensus expects FY27 revenue of $34.9B and EPS of $9.51, then FY28 revenue of $41B and EPS of $11.65; delivery on that ramp would bring the forward multiple of 25.9x FY28E earnings down to a level the growth supports.
Foundry demand led FY26 and is the near-term revenue driver; continued mature- and leading-edge foundry investment would extend the systems upcycle.
Customer support-related revenue grew {+ +20.2% +} in FY26; further growth in this installed-base stream would steady revenue between systems cycles.
Free cash flow of $4.9B in FY26 funded a capital-return program weighted to buybacks; sustained repurchases shrink the share count and support per-share value.
risks: China accounted for 34% of FY26 revenue; expanded U.S. export restrictions or Chinese retaliation would hit a material share of sales.
Wafer fabrication equipment demand is cyclical, as the FY24 downturn showed, and the steep consensus ramp penciled in for FY27 would be hard to sustain if the cycle turns.
The trailing multiple already prices in continued growth; a cut to forward estimates would compress both the multiple and the earnings base.
Memory fell to 39% of revenue from 42%; a slower memory recovery would remove one of the two main demand pillars.

financials.incomeCommentary: FY26 revenue was $23,232,690 thousand, up {+ +26.0% +} over FY25's $18,435,591 thousand, which the company attributes to strong demand for semiconductor equipment systems — particularly from foundry customers — plus customer support revenue. Gross margin rose to 50.5% from 48.7%, a {+ +180 bps +} gain the filing credits to favorable customer mix, partially offset by aluminum and steel tariff-related spend. Operating margin reached 35.3% and operating income $8.2B. Total operating expenses grew {+ +14.5% +} to $3,525,513 thousand, slower than revenue; within that, research and development was $2,375,873 thousand, or 10.2% of revenue (down from 11.4%), and SG&A $1,149,640 thousand. Net income rose {+ +35.6% +} to $7,265,396 thousand and diluted EPS {+ +38.8% +} to $5.76. The effective tax rate rose to 12.1% from 10.1%, which the company ties partly to the Global Minimum Tax taking full effect in fiscal 2026. The five-year path is cyclical, not linear: revenue fell {- -14.5% -} in FY24 before the FY25 and FY26 recovery, a reminder that the equipment cycle turns.
financials.balanceCommentary: Lam ended FY26 with cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash of about $5.60 billion, down from $6.41 billion a year earlier, against total debt of $3.7B — leaving a net cash position of roughly $1.9B. Total debt fell over the year as $750.0 million of Senior Notes matured in March 2026 and the company made $755.4 million of principal payments. Total equity was $12.5B and the current ratio 2.63, both consistent with a well-capitalized balance sheet. Deferred revenue declined to $2.43 billion from $2.68 billion, which the filing attributes mainly to lower customer down payments — worth watching as a soft read on forward orders, though one year's move is not a trend.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow was $5.86 billion in FY26, down from $6.17 billion in FY25 even as net income rose — a working-capital drag rather than an earnings problem. Capital expenditure was $966.4 million, up from the prior year, and free cash flow was $4.9B, an FCF margin of 21.1% versus 29.4% in FY25; the compression comes from the lower operating cash flow and higher capex together, not from weaker profitability. Free cash flow comfortably exceeded the $1.27 billion dividend, and the company also spent $3.85 billion on treasury stock purchases, including net share settlement of stock-based compensation. Total capital return therefore ran ahead of free cash flow, with the balance drawn from the cash pile, which fell over the year.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing earnings the shares are expensive: 52.4x FY26 EPS of $5.76 and 16.3x sales. The forward picture is where the debate sits — the stock trades at 31.7x the next twelve months' expected earnings and 25.9x the FY28E EPS of $11.65, multiples that look reasonable for a company the consensus expects to grow revenue to $34.9B in FY27 and $41B in FY28. The gap between the trailing and the forward multiple is entirely a function of those estimates; if the FY27–FY28 ramp disappoints, the forward multiple re-rates upward on a lower earnings base, and the trailing figure is what remains. We have no peer multiples in this pack and make no cross-sectional comparison; the read here is the company against its own history and its own forward estimates. EV/EBITDA is not available in the data.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The AI-driven equipment cycle runs longer than a normal upcycle, the consensus FY27–FY28 estimates (revenue $34.9B then $41B; EPS $9.51 then $11.65) are met or beaten, and the multiple holds near its recent premium, lifting the shares past their 52-week high.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Growth continues but decelerates from the FY26 +26.0% pace; the market pays roughly thirty times FY28 earnings as Lam converts a foundry-led order book, leaving the stock modestly above today's price.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Equipment cyclicality reasserts as it did in FY24 (revenue -14.5%), China trade restrictions (34% of FY26 revenue) or a memory pause cut the forward estimates, and the 52.4x trailing multiple compresses toward the low-20s on a reduced earnings base.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We frame three outcomes against the $301.83 close. In the Bull case ($445, 30% probability) the equipment cycle extends and the consensus FY27–FY28 estimates are met or beaten, taking the shares above their 52-week high. In the Base case ($350, 45%) growth continues but decelerates from the FY26 {+ +26.0% +} pace and the market pays roughly thirty times FY28 earnings, leaving the stock modestly above today's price. In the Bear case ($230, 25%) equipment cyclicality reasserts as it did in FY24, China restrictions or a memory pause cut the forward estimates, and the trailing multiple compresses on a reduced earnings base — a drop of about a quarter from the current price, which clears our requirement that the bear be a real scenario. The probabilities weight to a fair value modestly above the current price, an expected upside in the mid-teens against a bear-case downside near a quarter, for a reward-to-risk just below two-thirds. Our target range of $315 to $400 brackets the Base case.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Lam operates as a single business built around three process technologies — deposition, etch and clean — that are sequential, repeated steps in semiconductor fabrication. It disaggregates revenue two ways that describe the model without being reportable segments: by type, systems revenue of $14,885,488 thousand (new leading-edge equipment) against customer support-related revenue and other of $8,347,202 thousand (services, spares, upgrades and non-leading-edge Reliant equipment); and by end market, foundry at 54% of FY26 revenue, memory at 39% and logic/IDM at 7%. The customer-support stream, tied to a broad installed base, is the more recurring half and grew {+ +20.2% +} in FY26.

moatFactors.name: Installed base and support
moatFactors.body: Customer support-related revenue — services, spares and upgrades on equipment already in the field — is the recurring-leaning half of the model and grew again in FY26. The 10-K cites the ability to leverage 'cycles of learning from our broad installed base' as a source of differentiation. This stream cushions the systems cycle.

moatFactors.name: Deposition, etch and clean breadth
moatFactors.body: The company describes its position as 'leadership and expertise in deposition, etch, and clean markets,' spanning product families the 10-K names across all three steps — deposition (ALTUS, SABRE, VECTOR), etch (Akara, Kiyo, Vantex, Syndion) and clean (Coronus, Da Vinci). Breadth across the three sequential steps raises switching costs for customers integrating a process flow.

moatFactors.name: R&D intensity
moatFactors.body: Research and development was $2,375,873 thousand in FY26, 10.2% of revenue, funding leading-edge deposition, etch and clean development. Sustained R&D is the price of staying on the technology inflections — 3D scaling, advanced patterning, new materials — that the company says drive demand for its equipment.

moatFactors.name: Margin structure
moatFactors.body: Gross margin reached 50.5% and operating margin 35.3% in FY26, both up year over year, evidence of pricing and mix power in the core franchise. Margins at this level on $23.2B of revenue point to a business not competing primarily on price.

businessMoat.durability: The moat rests on process know-how, an installed base that generates recurring support revenue, and breadth across the deposition, etch and clean steps that customers integrate into a single flow — none of which turns over quickly. The durability question is technological: the 10-K itself warns that future technologies or processes, 'including as a result of adoption of AI,' could render current offerings obsolete or let customers reduce their reliance on Lam for process development. Competition is described as coming from multiple established competitors and 'new, regional competitors,' alongside the risk that customers adopt approaches that reduce their reliance on Lam for process development. The moat is wide today; the watch item is whether a technology inflection or a new competitor erodes it over the next cycle.

points: FY26 revenue grew {+ +26.0% +} to $23.2B, the second consecutive up year after the FY24 downturn, led by foundry demand.
Systems revenue rose {+ +29.5% +} to $14,885,488 thousand on foundry equipment spending; customer support-related revenue rose {+ +20.2% +} to $8,347,202 thousand.
The foundry share of revenue climbed to 54% from 45% (+900 bps), while memory eased to 39% from 42% and logic/IDM to 7%.
Consensus estimates step up sharply: FY27 revenue of $34.9B and EPS of $9.51, then FY28 revenue of $41B and EPS of $11.65 — the engine of the forward multiple, and the main thing to prove out.
Margins widened with volume: gross margin {+ +180 bps +} to 50.5% and operating margin to 35.3%, so revenue growth is dropping through to earnings — diluted EPS rose {+ +38.8% +} to $5.76.

management.leadership: Timothy M. Archer is President and Chief Executive Officer, Douglas R. Bettinger is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, and Patrick J. Lord is Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer, per the FY2025 proxy's list of named executive officers. The same list names Ava A. Harter as Chief Legal Officer, who joined in July 2024, and Seshasayee Varadarajan as head of the Global Products Group. The pack carries no execution commentary beyond the financial results, so we judge the team on those: FY26 delivered revenue growth of {+ +26.0% +} and margin expansion, with operating expenses growing slower than revenue.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation in FY26 favored buybacks: $3.85 billion of treasury stock purchases, including net share settlement of stock-based compensation, against $1.27 billion of dividends, funded from $5.86 billion of operating cash flow. The company also retired debt, with $750.0 million of Senior Notes maturing in March 2026 and $755.4 million of principal payments, taking total debt down to $3.7B against a net cash position. The dividend yields 0.46% at the current price — a small direct payout, with the buyback the larger lever. Returning more than free cash flow in a single year is sustainable here given the net-cash balance sheet, but bears watching if operating cash flow stays below net income.
management.governance: The FY2025 proxy states that all current directors other than Mr. Archer are independent under Nasdaq criteria, and that the audit, compensation, and nominating and governance committees are composed entirely of independent directors. An independent director, Abhijit Y. Talwalkar, serves as chair of the Board; because the chair is independent, the Board has not designated a separate lead independent director. The proxy reports no family relationships among directors and officers and no related-party transaction above the $120,000 threshold during fiscal 2025, other than noting Lam's investments in BlackRock money-market funds — BlackRock is a 5% holder — from which it received about $26.7 million in interest and dividends. Governance reads as standard for a large-cap Nasdaq issuer.
management.insiderOwnership: As of the September 5, 2025 record date, all current directors and executive officers as a group held 3,971,889 shares, less than 1% of the 1,261,032,300 shares outstanding — modest insider ownership typical of a long-public large cap. CEO Timothy Archer held 1,481,175 shares. Institutional ownership is concentrated in The Vanguard Group at 10.24% and BlackRock at 9.34%. There is no controlling shareholder.

idiosyncratic: China concentration: 34% of FY26 revenue shipped to China. Tighter U.S. export controls on advanced equipment, Chinese retaliation, or a preference for domestic toolmakers would strike a market that is more than a third of sales; the 10-K flags 'new, regional competitors' as a rising pressure.

Cyclicality: wafer fabrication equipment spending is cyclical, and Lam's own five-year history shows revenue falling {- -14.5% -} in FY24. The current up-leg has lifted both the shares and the multiple; a downturn would compress both.

Estimate risk: consensus expects FY27 revenue of $34.9B, roughly a 50% increase, and EPS of $9.51. The forward multiple that makes the stock look reasonable depends on that ramp; a cut would re-rate the shares on a lower base.

Foundry concentration: foundry rose to 54% of FY26 revenue while memory fell to 39%. Heavy reliance on a small number of leading-edge foundry customers means an investment pause at one of them moves the top line.
risks.systemic: Lam's fortunes track the semiconductor capital-equipment cycle, which in turn tracks end demand for chips across mobile, computing, data-center and automotive markets and the capacity decisions of a handful of large manufacturers. A broad slowdown in electronics demand, a memory glut, or a pullback in AI-related data-center investment would reduce wafer fabrication equipment spending industry-wide, independent of Lam's execution. Trade policy is a systemic overlay: the 10-K cites trade restrictions and tariffs as factors that have had, and may again have, a negative impact on revenue and operating margin, and aluminum and steel tariffs already showed up as a drag on FY26 gross margin. These are conditions Lam manages but does not control.

body: We rate Lam Research a BUY. FY26 paired double-digit revenue growth with margin expansion and a step-up in earnings, delivered by a business with a wide moat in deposition, etch and clean, a recurring support stream, and a net-cash balance sheet returning cash through buybacks and dividends. The probability-weighted fair value from our scenarios sits modestly above the current price.

The reason we stop at BUY rather than a stronger call, and sit below the Street's $373.13 target, is valuation against cyclicality: 52.4x trailing earnings leaves little margin for error, the forward multiple depends on a steep FY27–FY28 ramp the consensus has penciled in, and 34% China exposure plus the FY24 revenue decline are reminders that this industry turns. Our $315 to $400 target range brackets the base case; we would add on weakness toward the lower end and trim into a move toward the bull case.
